title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Trichoblastomas and trichoepitheliomas are benign hair-germ tumors that most commonly arise on the face and scalp of adults. They may mimic basal cell carcinoma, among other cutaneous adnexal tumors, clinically and warrant histopathologic evaluation. Although these lesions most often appear sporadically, they are sometimes associated with familial genetic syndromes. The exact incidence and prevalence of TE/TB in the general population (as well as familial genetic syndromes) are not known, but cases are rare. Most sporadic lesions present in adults aged 40 or older. This activity illustrates the evaluation of these lesions and highlights the role of the healthcare team in their management.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Summarize histopathologic findings of trichoblastomas and trichoepitheliomas. Identify differential diagnoses for trichoblastomas and trichoepitheliomas. Review treatment modalities that may be considered for patients with either solitary or multiple trichoblastomas or trichoepitheliomas. Explain the relationship between trichoblastomas and trichoepitheliomas, as well as their associated familial genetic conditions. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Introduction
content: Trichoblastoma and trichoepithelioma are benign hair-germ tumors that most commonly arise on the face and scalp of adults (see Image. Trichoblastoma). Brooke first described trichoepithelioma as epithelioma adenoides cysticum in 1892. In 1953, Pinkus further modified his description, and in 1967, Lever and Montgomery independently reported that embryonic origins are present within pluripotent hair follicle germ cells. [1]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Introduction
content: Trichoblastoma was first described in 1970 by Headington as a differentiated follicular neoplasm and was further characterized by Ackerman et al in 1993 to include all benign hair-germ cell tumors. [2] Although trichoepithelioma and trichoblastoma are 2 distinct entities, the former may be considered a subset of the latter. [3] Trichoepitheliomas/trichoblastomas are benign and rarely metastasize. However, they can transform into trichoblastic carcinoma (TBC), which arises from loss of the p53 tumor suppressor protein and elevated PI3K-AKT signaling in tumor cells. TBC has more potential for local invasion, recurrence, and metastasis. [4]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Epidemiology
content: The exact incidence and prevalence of trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma in the general population (as well as in familial genetic syndromes) are unknown, but cases are rare. Most sporadic lesions present in adults aged 40 or older. [3] Brooke-Spiegler syndrome predominantly affects young women (male-to-female ratio of 1:6-9.6).

content: Patients with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome may also have spiradenomas and cylindromas. MFT is a phenotypic variant of this condition characterized by numerous trichoepitheliomas primarily located on the nasolabial folds and inner eyebrows. [7]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Pathophysiology
content: The etiology and pathophysiology of trichoepithelioma and trichoblastoma remain incompletely understood. Trichoepithelioma arises from epithelial-mesenchymal cells, and multiple trichoepitheliomas may be associated with a familial genetic condition known as multiple familial trichoepithelioma (MFT). MFT is a disorder associated with 2 autosomal-dominant mutations in tumor suppressor genes. The first gene is on chromosome 9q21. [5]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Pathophysiology
content: The second is the cylindromatous tumor suppressor gene (CYLD) on chromosome 16q12-q13, which is also the gene implicated in Brooke-Spiegler syndrome. [6] This leads to loss of function of the deubiquitinating enzyme CYLD, thereby elevating NF-κB signaling. These patients present with multiple trichoblastomas beginning in adolescence/early adulthood. [1] Like trichoblastoma, most cases of tricholemmoma present sporadically and in isolation. Most solitary trichoblastoma lesions are associated with mutations at 9q22.3. [2]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Histopathology
content: Trichoepithelioma and trichoblastoma are 2 common benign histologic mimickers of basal cell carcinoma. Histologically, trichoblastoma appears as a sizable dermal tumor without connection to the epidermis. It is well-circumscribed and composed of primitive basaloid cells that may arrange in multiple large or small nodules.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Histopathology
content: Trichoepithelioma appears similar to trichoblastoma; however, tumor cells appear more mature, may be accompanied by horn cysts (ie, foci of excessive keratinization), and are connected to the epidermis. Both trichoepithelioma and trichoblastoma exhibit peripheral palisading and spindled-fibroblast follicular stroma without mucin. Papillary mesenchymal bodies (tumor-cupping oval stromal blebs) are not always seen; when seen, they are specific for benign hair germ-cell tumors. [8]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Histopathology
content: A histologic variant of trichoepithelioma is desmoplastic trichoepithelioma (DTE), which presents with narrow strands of basaloid cells accompanied by keratinized horn cysts and fibrous, desmoplastic stroma (see Image. Desmoplastic Trichoepithelioma). [9]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Histopathology
content: Multiple histologic variants of trichoblastoma exist according to the updated 2018 World Health Organization (WHO) "Skin Tumors" classification, including nodular, retiform, cribriform, racemiform, and columnar. Less common variants of trichoblastoma include clear cell, pigmented, and adamantinoid. Furthermore, dermatopathologists may recognize trichoepithelioma as a variant of trichoblastoma characterized by smaller tumor nodules, more superficial clusters of cells, and abundant fibrotic stroma. "Conventional" and "desmoplastic" trichoepithelioma may also be reported as "cribriform" and "columnar" trichoepithelioma, respectively. Another rare adamantine variant of trichoblastoma has been described and termed cutaneous lymphadenoma due to prominent lymphocytic infiltrates within tumor nests. [10]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- History and Physical
content: Typically, trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma presents as small (0.2-1 cm) skin-colored, slow-growing papules or nodules, similar to BCC. They often appear on the head (face or scalp) but may be found on the trunk or extremities. [11] Other locations on the body may be affected, too, such as the vulva, and it is not uncommon for lesions to appear without other cutaneous neoplasms (eg, inverted follicular keratosis, syringocystadenoma papilliferum). [10]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- History and Physical
content: Rarely, trichoblastoma may arise in nevus sebaceus (of Jadassohn), which may present as a translucent, verrucous plaque with central nodularity and pigmentation. [12] On the other hand, DTE often presents as white-to-yellow, firm skin-colored papules, plaques, or nodules with a central indentation on the face or cheeks. [9]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- History and Physical
content: Patients with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome typically present with multiple nodules (ranging from 10 to several hundred) that resemble BCCs on the head and neck, measuring 0.5-3.0 cm. Multiple confluent lesions involving the scalp may form a “turban tumor.” Rapid enlargement and bleeding may suggest malignant transformation, which occurs in about 5 to 10% of cases. [13] MFT presents with multiple skin-colored papules and nodules, although they may be smaller (5-10 mm) and are mainly distributed to the inner eyebrows and nasolabial folds. [14]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Evaluation
content: Evaluation of trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma begins with obtaining the patient's history and performing a thorough physical examination. Histopathologic examination via skin biopsy is critical because these lesions can clinically resemble BCC and other adnexal tumors. Due to overlapping histopathologic features, IHC evaluation may be needed. Dermoscopy is unlikely to be of further help, as these lesions demonstrate dermoscopic findings such as arborizing vessels, gray ovoid nests, and globules. [10] A genetic workup may be necessary for patients with multiple or recurrent lesions, including evaluation of chromosome 9q21 (for MFT) or the CYLD gene (for Brooke-Spiegler syndrome). [15]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Treatment / Management
content: Solitary trichoepithelioma/trichoblastomas are benign and are cured with complete surgical excision. Multiple lesions, especially on the face (as seen with genetic syndromes), are more challenging to address. Mohs surgery may be warranted at centrofacial sites, particularly in variants with deep dermal or subdermal infiltration. [16]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Treatment / Management
content: Frequent facial surgery may be disfiguring (ie, scarring) and cause significant distress. Furthermore, multiple trichoepithelioma/trichoblastomas associated with underlying genetic familial syndromes may recur after surgery, leaving numerous scars and invasive treatments throughout a patient’s lifetime.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Treatment / Management
content: There is no universally accepted guideline or protocol for the treatment of multiple trichoepitheliomas/trichoblastomas. Other than surgical excision, treatment options, such as electrosurgery, dermabrasion, cryotherapy, and radiation therapy, are limited and invasive. Moreover, radiation therapy is associated with an increased risk of other skin cancers. Besides scarring, pain, bleeding, infection, and lesion recurrence are additional risks of these and other invasive surgical therapies.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Treatment / Management
content: Laser treatments (such as carbon dioxide, erbium:YAG, and diode) may rapidly remove many lesions safely and effectively, without recurrence or cosmetic morbidity. Although they may be minimally invasive, frequent treatments may result in hypertrophic scarring, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation, and local skin-site inflammatory changes (eg, edema, erythema, ulceration, burning).

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Treatment / Management
content: Other pharmacologic agents may be considered, such as sirolimus, imiquimod, tretinoin, vismodegib, aspirin, and adalimumab. However, further clinical trials are warranted as current evidence for these and other medical therapies is anecdotal. [17]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The primary differential diagnosis is nodular BCC. Tumor cells have elongated nuclei and show prominent palisading along the periphery of the tumor nodules, which often extends into the dermis. Major cleft retraction, cytologic atypia, significant mitotic activity, tumor necrosis, or myxoinflammatory stroma may be present. Trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma often lacks these features. However, similar to trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma, BCC tends to arise in sun-exposed areas (eg, face, neck, head).

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: In challenging cases, cytokeratin 20 (CK20) can distinguish trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma from BCC, as this marker routinely stains Merkel cells in benign hair-germ tumors. This stain may be used alongside androgen receptor (AR) staining when evaluating trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma versus BCC, as AR positivity (with CK20 negativity) supports the diagnosis of BCC. However, AR positivity may be focal or completely absent in some cases of BCC. [8]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: DTE may histologically appear similar to the morpheaphorm subtype of BCC (MBCC), other adnexal tumors (eg, syringoma, microcystic adnexal carcinoma - MAC), and cutaneous metastatic breast cancer. IHC staining may sometimes help in tumor differentiation; however, correlation with clinical and histologic features remains essential. As opposed to these other entities, DTE routinely expresses CK20-positive Merkel cells.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Although multiple histologic variants of trichoblastoma are recognized in the updated 2018 WHO classification guidelines, CD34 (stromal), BCL-2, CK20, and PHLDA1 positivity may be used to distinguish trichoblastoma from BCC. [10] Additionally, trichoblastomas often lack patch (PTCH) gene mutations, which are commonly seen in BCC, particularly in syndromic variants. [18]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FeP) is an uncommon BCC variant that may resemble trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma. Histology of FeP often shows fenestrated strands of basaloid epithelial tumor cells with significant dermal fibrosis. Peripheral palisading of fenestrations tends to be apparent, and stromal clefting with tumor cell retraction is common. FeP often stains positive for CK20 (85% of cases), AR (77% of cases), and BCL-2. [19]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Another entity that clinically resembles BCC and trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma is basaloid follicular hamartoma (BFH), a rare benign adnexal tumor. Like BCC, BFH arises from a PTCH mutation located on chromosome 9q23. This gene encodes a receptor for the sonic hedgehog pathway, and mutations lead to abnormal tumor cell growth and development (see Image. Trichoblastoma Path). However, BFH classically centers around hair follicles and remains limited to the superficial dermis. Branching cords of basaloid cells can be seen connecting to pilosebaceous units in early disease, and tumor cells may completely replace them in cases of longstanding disease. [20]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis for solitary trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma is excellent. However, the likelihood of lesion recurrence dramatically increases in patients with familial genetic syndromes. Since these lesions predominantly appear in the face or neck, healthcare providers must consider the time, costs, and morbidity associated with frequent invasive treatments. [17]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Complications
content: As trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma are benign entities, surgical excision is curative with a minimal likelihood of disease recurrence or metastasis. Complications of surgery, other invasive treatments, and laser treatments are discussed in the “Treatment/Management” section of this topic.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: In cases of solitary lesions, treatment and management of trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma are relatively unremarkable, given the benign nature of these tumors. However, in familial genetic syndromes, treatment plans may be more complex due to the risk of lesion recurrence, assortment, and location in cosmetically sensitive areas (eg, face).

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients with multiple lesions or a suggestive family history should communicate this with their providers as further genetic workup may be necessary. Practitioners should also reassure patients that trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma is benign and distinct from BCC.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Histopathologic evaluation of cutaneous adnexal tumors, such as trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma, is essential for accurate diagnosis and subsequent patient management. As with many conditions, the clinicopathologic correlation between biopsy findings and patient presentation is critical when selecting the most likely diagnoses and the optimal next management steps.

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Given that trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma is a frequent mimicker of BCC (both clinically and histologically), a single biopsy may be insufficient in some cases. If a patient presents with more extensive or multiple skin tumors that may be concerning for BCC versus trichoepithelioma/trichoblastoma versus other entities, obtaining several biopsies (either from the same or various tumors) may be best. Given the potential for malignant transformation of trichoepithelioma and trichoblastoma, complete excision of benign lesions with negative margins is recommended. [21]

title: Trichoblastoma and Trichoepithelioma -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
